dilatational-force-density-term.title: Dilatational Force Density Term
dilatational-force-density-term.conceptual_definition: This vector term represents the contribution to the internal force density within a deformable continuum that arises from the spatial variation of its volumetric strain (dilatation), scaled by the sum of the first Lamé parameter and the shear modulus.
dilatational-force-density-term.intuitive_summary: It describes how local changes in volume (expansion or compression) within a material generate internal forces that tend to propagate and equalize these volumetric deformations across the medium.
dilatational-force-density-term.interpretation:
In the context of linear elasticity, this term, $(\lambda + \mu) 
abla ( 
abla \cdot \mathbf{v})$, is a component of the total elastic force density acting on a material element. Here, $\mathbf{v} typically represents the displacement field. The divergence of the displacement field, $
abla \cdot $\mathbf{v}$, quantifies the local volumetric change or dilatation. The gradient of this dilatation, $
abla ( 
abla \cdot \mathbf{v})$, indicates how this volumetric change varies spatially. If a region is expanding or compressing differently from an adjacent one, this term contributes a force that tends to smooth out these volumetric differences. The coefficients $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are the Lamé parameters, which are material constants characterizing the isotropic elastic medium's resistance to compression and shear, respectively. Their sum $(\lambda + \mu)$ scales the magnitude of this dilatational force contribution. An analogous term appears in the Navier-Stokes equations for compressible fluids, where $\mathbf{v} is the velocity field and $\lambda, \mu$ are related to bulk and shear viscosities, representing viscous forces due to volumetric changes.
dilatational-force-density-term.symmetry_origin: This term originates from the constitutive relations for isotropic linear elastic materials or Newtonian fluids, which are invariant under rotations and reflections. The Lamé parameters $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are scalar material constants that define this isotropic response. The vector operator $\nabla ( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v})$ is constructed from scalar and vector differential operators, ensuring that the resulting force density is a vector field consistent with the underlying spatial symmetries of the continuum mechanics equations.
dilatational-force-density-term.limits_and_boundary: **Incompressible Limit:** For an incompressible material, the divergence of the displacement (or velocity) field, $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, is zero. In this limit, the entire term vanishes, as there are no volumetric changes to generate such forces. This often implies that $\lambda \to \infty$ in elasticity, but the product $\lambda ( \nabla \cdot $\mathbf{v}$)$ remains finite, typically manifesting as a pressure term. **Static Equilibrium:** In static equilibrium, if this term is part of a force balance equation, it must be balanced by other forces (e.g., pressure gradients, other elastic forces, or external body forces). **Boundary Conditions:** At material interfaces or boundaries, the continuity of displacement (for elasticity) or velocity (for fluids) and the balance of forces (stress vectors) would dictate the behavior and contribution of this term.

lambda.name: First Lamé Parameter
lambda.description: A material constant representing the resistance to volumetric change (compression or expansion) in an isotropic elastic medium. In fluid dynamics, it can be related to the bulk viscosity.

mu.name: Second Lamé Parameter
mu.description: A material constant representing the resistance to shear deformation in an isotropic elastic medium, also known as the shear modulus. In fluid dynamics, it represents the dynamic shear viscosity.

nabla.name: Nabla Operator
nabla.description: A vector differential operator that, when applied to a scalar field, produces a vector field pointing in the direction of the greatest rate of increase of the scalar field. When applied as part of the divergence operator, it measures the local expansion or contraction of a vector field.

v.name: Displacement Field
v.description: A vector field representing the displacement of material points from their equilibrium positions in elasticity. In fluid dynamics, it represents the local velocity of fluid particles, in which case its unit would be m/s.
